content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler fruit and meat (4122) is a ready‑to‑eat baby food that combines carefully selected fruits and lean meat, designed for children aged 6 months to 3 years. The product is gently heat‑treated to retain most vitamins and minerals, has a smooth texture and a pleasant taste, making the transition from breast‑feeding to solid foods easier.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The fruit‑meat blend provides a wide range of nutrients in a single serving.
Made from 100 % natural ingredients with no artificial colours, flavours or preservatives.
Fruits (apple, pear, banana) are rich in vitamins C and A, while the meat (turkey, chicken) supplies high‑quality protein and iron.
Low‑temperature processing preserves most bioactive compounds.
Packaged in safe, reusable food‑grade plastic.

items.title: Supports growth and development
items.content: The combination of meat protein and fruit vitamins promotes normal tissue growth, muscle development and nervous system maturation in toddlers.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: Vitamin C from fruits and zinc from meat help strengthen the immune system and increase resistance to infections.

items.title: Digestive health
items.content: Fruit dietary fibre supports regular bowel movements and helps prevent constipation.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Natural fruit sugars provide a quick source of energy, while protein offers sustained satiety.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Meat provides easily absorbable iron, important for preventing anemia in young children.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Children may be allergic to individual ingredients (e.g., chicken or certain fruits). Observe for reactions when first introducing the product.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although the sugar is natural, children prone to dental caries should have the product offered in moderation.

items.title: Not suitable for infants under 6 months
items.content: Because of texture and composition, the product is intended only for babies older than six months.

items.title: Post‑opening storage
items.content: After opening, keep the container refrigerated and use within 48 hours to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve at room temperature. It can be warmed to about 37 °C in the microwave (10‑15 seconds), then mixed well before offering to the child. If a thinner consistency is needed, add a small amount of breast milk or formula.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight, not exceeding 25 °C. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 48 hours. Discard if you notice off‑odors, colour changes or altered texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a tender, lean poultry meat rich in high‑quality protein, B‑vitamins, and essential minerals. For toddlers it provides a valuable source of energy and supports proper muscle and nervous system development. It is usually served as a puree or finely shredded pieces, prepared without added salt or strong spices.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey contains less fat than chicken and virtually no cholesterol.
It is high in tryptophan, an amino acid involved in serotonin production, which may help promote a good mood.
Turkey is considered a "gentle" meat and is often introduced to babies after 6–12 months of age.
Unlike red meat, turkey provides non‑heme iron that is easily absorbed when paired with vitamin‑C‑rich vegetables.

items.title: Rich in high‑quality protein
items.content: Easily digestible protein supports the growth of muscle tissue in young children.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey supplies vitamin B6 and niacin (B3), which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Essential minerals
items.content: Contains phosphorus, selenium and zinc – key for bone health, immune function and hormonal balance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Its leanness helps keep the overall calorie density of a toddler’s diet moderate.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: Selenium provides antioxidant protection for cells.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some children may develop an allergic reaction to poultry; introduce gradually and monitor for symptoms.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Turkey must be cooked thoroughly to eliminate salmonella and campylobacter.

items.title: Texture
items.content: For infants under 12 months the meat should be pureed to avoid choking hazards.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Do not add salt, as a toddler’s kidneys are not yet efficient at excreting sodium.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steam, boil or bake turkey without added fat, then blend into a smooth puree. You can mix in a small amount of vegetable puree (e.g., carrot or pumpkin) for flavor and extra nutrients. For older toddlers, serve finely shredded pieces mixed into cereal or rice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared puree in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 1 month. Thaw in the fridge, not at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Cooked calamari is a seafood product obtained after a short heat treatment of the body of cephalopod mollusks. It has a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a tender yet firm texture. Calamari is commonly used in salads, appetizers, pastas, and rice dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Calamari belong to the class Cephalopoda and are relatives of octopuses and cuttlefish.
Calamari flesh is composed of about 80 % water.
They can change skin colour thanks to pigment cells called chromatophores.
In Japan, cooked calamari is often served with soy sauce and wasabi.
There are more than 300 species of calamari, but only a few are widely used in cuisine.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Calamari provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many seafoods, cooked calamari contains little fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Calamari is a good source of selenium, zinc and copper, important for immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids and vitamin A in calamari help maintain good vision.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to calamari, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Calamari is rich in purines, so people with gout should limit consumption.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Marine products can contain heavy metals and toxins; purchase from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked calamari can be sliced into rings or strips and added to salads, pasta, rice rolls, or served as an appetizer with lemon juice and olive oil. It also works well in hot dishes where it quickly reheats without losing tenderness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked calamari in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze it in a sealed bag, where it keeps quality for up to 3 months. Before use, check for off‑odors – a sour or rancid smell indicates spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Johnnycake is a traditional American flatbread made from cornmeal, water and salt. The batter is cooked on a skillet or baked until a golden crust forms. Johnnycake has a dense, slightly crumbly texture and a distinctive corn flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Johnnycake originated in New England in the 17th century as a simple way to use cornmeal brought by European settlers.
The name "johnnycake" is thought to derive from "journey cake," highlighting its convenience for travelers.
In different U.S. regions the bread is known by various names: "hoecake," "corn cake," or "syrup cake."
Traditionally it was served with maple syrup, butter, or fried bacon.
Some recipes add milk, eggs or leavening agents for a softer crumb.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Cornmeal provides slow‑releasing energy, helping to keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Corn contains dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Gluten‑free (when made with pure cornmeal)
items.content: Johnnycake can be a safe option for people with celiac disease if prepared with gluten‑free cornmeal.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Cornmeal supplies thiamine, niacin and folate, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The classic recipe contains no added oil, making it a relatively low‑calorie food.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Cornmeal can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should consume johnnycake in moderation.

items.title: Low protein content
items.content: Compared with many grains, cornmeal is low in protein, so the dish may need additional protein sources for a balanced meal.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot johnnycake spread with butter, maple syrup, honey or jam. It can also be cut into cubes for sandwiches, added to salads, or served alongside fried meats.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked johnnycake in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in the oven or skillet before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Luncheon meat, loaf type (1013) is a solid, fully cooked meat product formed into a loaf shape. It is made from selected meat cuts (usually pork and beef), salt, spices and often includes curing agents such as nitrites to preserve color and extend shelf life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “loaf” refers to the bread‑like shape of the product.
In many post‑Soviet countries this product is commonly called “meat loaf” or simply “loaf”.
It is a popular base for sandwiches, cold platters and salads.
Flavor enhancers like garlic, paprika or mustard powder are sometimes added.
The solid form makes it easy to slice thinly for school cafeterias and catering.

items.title: Source of high‑quality protein
items.content: Provides essential animal protein needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Provides heme iron, which is readily absorbed and supports oxygen transport.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Supplies B12, B6 and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: Contribute to bone and dental health.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb dietary patterns.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The product is often heavily salted, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Some additives can cause allergic reactions or increase the formation of nitrosamines with long‑term consumption.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: May contain significant saturated fat, a consideration for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Individuals with specific meat allergies should avoid it.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the loaf thinly for sandwiches, salads, snack platters or enjoy it as a quick bite. It can be served cold or gently warmed in a pan or microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C in the original packaging or an airtight container. Once opened, consume within 5–7 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C or below.

manicotti-cheese-filled-with-meat-sauce.title: Manicotti with Cheese and Meat Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Manicotti are large tube-shaped pasta shells stuffed with creamy cheese and baked under a savory meat sauce. The durum‑wheat dough holds its shape during baking, while the cheese filling adds a smooth, rich texture. The meat sauce is typically made from ground beef, tomatoes, onion, and herbs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the Italian “manicotto,” meaning “sleeve.”
Traditionally the filling is ricotta, but modern versions use mozzarella, parmesan, or even vegetarian cheeses.
The dish is a staple at family gatherings and Italian restaurants as a baked casserole.
The tubular shape helps trap sauce inside the pasta.
In Italy manicotti are often served “baked manicotti,” topped with melted mozzarella.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Cheese and beef provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus
items.content: The cheese contributes calcium and phosphorus, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat sauce supplies B12, B6, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes in the sauce are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that helps protect cells.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Durum‑wheat pasta provides slowly digestible carbs for steady energy release.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The dish is rich in fats and carbs, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Lactose presence
items.content: Cheese may cause discomfort for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Prepared sauce often contains added salt; those with hypertension should choose a low‑sodium version.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional pasta contains wheat gluten and is unsuitable for those with celiac disease; gluten‑free pasta can be used as a substitute.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve manicotti hot, sprinkled with grated parmesan and fresh herbs. They pair well with a light arugula salad or a side of roasted vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months. Reheat until the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

potato-mashed-from-dry-mix-made-with-mil.title: Mashed potatoes from dry mix, made with milk, with gravy

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potatoes from a dry mix, prepared with milk and gravy, is a convenient ready‑to‑eat product that quickly reproduces the taste of homemade mash. The dry mix contains dehydrated potatoes, powdered milk components and spices, while the gravy adds a rich, savory flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dry mixes allow the product to be stored for long periods without quality loss.
Preparation usually takes 5‑7 minutes after boiling water and adding milk.
Gravy is often made from meat broth, making the dish more filling.
Many mixes are fortified with B‑vitamins and iron.
In several countries these mixes are a staple in school cafeterias.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Potatoes provide complex carbohydrates that supply sustained energy.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: Milk added to the mix boosts calcium and vitamin D, supporting bone health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Dry mixes typically contain little fat unless butter is added separately.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: The product often includes vitamin C and B6, which aid immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The smooth texture makes it suitable for children and people with chewing difficulties.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some mixes have high salt levels, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: The product contains milk, so those with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy should choose a dairy‑free version.

items.title: Additives and preservatives
items.content: Dry mixes may contain food additives that are not suitable for everyone.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Mashed potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour boiling water over the mix, add milk and stir until smooth, then serve with prepared gravy. Butter, cheese or herbs can be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dry mix in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. Prepared mash should be consumed within 2‑3 hours; leftovers can be refrigerated for up to one day.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice cooked with coconut milk is a fragrant side dish where each grain absorbs the creamy flavor of coconut. The coconut milk gives the dish a smooth, velvety texture and a subtle sweetness, making it popular in Asian and Caribbean cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coconut milk contains lauric acid, which gives its distinctive aroma and may support the immune system.
Traditionally, coconut rice is prepared in Thailand, Indonesia, and the Maldives.
The rice‑coconut combination has been used in ancient rituals as a symbol of abundance.
The dish is often served with mango, pineapple, or toasted peanuts for flavor contrast.
Coconut milk can be made from fresh coconut flesh or purchased in canned form.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Coconut milk provides medium‑chain triglycerides that are quickly metabolized and can serve as an immediate energy source.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Together, coconut milk and rice deliver a high amount of potassium, supporting normal blood pressure.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in rice combined with enzymes in coconut milk promotes healthy gastrointestinal function.

items.title: Antioxidant effect
items.content: Lauric acid and phenolic compounds in coconut have antioxidant properties that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune‑boosting
items.content: Lauric acid in coconut milk can be converted in the body to monolaurin, which has antiviral activity.

items.title: Coconut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to coconut milk, ranging from skin rashes to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Coconut milk is high in saturated fats; people with elevated cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The combination of rice and coconut milk makes the dish calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable for weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Copper and iron balance
items.content: Large amounts of coconut milk can increase copper intake, which in excess may interfere with iron absorption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Coconut rice is served as a side to curries, seafood, or grilled meats. It can also be used in desserts such as tropical puddings, or paired with fresh fruit and nuts. For extra brightness add a pinch of salt, lime zest, or grated ginger.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat by steaming or microwaving, adding a splash of coconut milk to restore its creamy texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Flour tortilla is a thin, flexible flatbread made from wheat flour, water, salt, and sometimes a small amount of fat. It is a staple of Mexican cuisine, used for tacos, burritos, quesadillas and many other dishes. The dough is rolled into round discs and quickly cooked on a dry skillet or grill.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat tortillas originated in the northern regions of Mexico where wheat grew better than corn.
Compared with corn tortillas, wheat versions are softer and more pliable, making them ideal for wrapping fillings.
Traditionally tortillas were hand‑rolled on a stone surface called a “tacita”.
In the United States wheat tortillas became popular in the 1920s thanks to Mexican restaurants and fast‑food chains.
Tortillas can be kept in the refrigerator for up to a week and frozen for up to three months.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Tortillas provide a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Wheat flour in tortillas adds fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Provides B‑vitamins
items.content: Tortillas contain thiamine, niacin and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When cooked without added oil, tortillas have a modest fat content.

items.title: Convenient way to add vegetables
items.content: Tortillas make it easy to incorporate vegetables, beans and lean proteins into meals.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat tortillas contain gluten and are unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because the carbs are rapidly absorbed, tortillas can raise blood sugar levels, which is relevant for diabetics.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some commercial tortillas contain added salt; choose low‑sodium options when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use tortillas as a base for tacos, burritos, quesadillas, fajitas and wraps. Heat them on a dry skillet, in the microwave or in the oven. Thin tortillas work well for rolls, while thicker ones are good for baked dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store tortillas in an airtight bag at room temperature for up to 5 days. For longer storage keep them refrigerated for up to 2 weeks or frozen for up to 3 months. Warm before use to restore flexibility.
